caption:
Microsoft unveiled new in-house AI models at Ignite on Tuesday, led by MAI Code 2 for programming.
Microsoft says the models come close to rivals from OpenAI and Anthropic at a fraction of the cost.
The pitch to businesses: cheaper AI agents that run all day.

Would you switch coding models to save money?

threads_text: Microsoft just unveiled MAI Code 2 and a set of cheaper in-house AI models, pitched straight at OpenAI and Anthropic customers. The message is not that it beats everyone, but that it is close enough for far less money. Would you trade a little quality for a much smaller AI bill?

paragraphs.text: Microsoft unveiled a group of new in-house AI models on November 17, 2026, at its Ignite conference in San Francisco, positioning them as lower-cost alternatives to models from Anthropic and OpenAI, Reuters reported.

The lineup includes MAI Code 2, a model for computer programming that Microsoft says nearly matches the performance of rival models at a fraction of the cost. Yahoo Finance reported that the model is built for complex, time-consuming programming work, can operate across multiple files and understands entire software projects.

Microsoft also introduced a model built for cybersecurity, which it plans to offer to a limited group of customers. Reuters said it is meant to help with the growing number of software vulnerabilities that AI tools are uncovering. The company released image generation and transcription models as well.

WindowsForum, citing Neowin, Axios and the GitHub changelog, listed the main pieces as MAI Code 2, a lighter MAI Code 2 Flash, MAI Cyber 2 Flash for security agents, MAI Image 2.7 for image generation and editing, MAI Realtime 1 for speech and a healthcare transcription product built on MAI Transcribe 2. Axios counted six new model families.

According to the figures WindowsForum reported from Microsoft, MAI Code 2 reaches 96 percent of the performance of Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 at 5 percent of the cost, and 98 percent of OpenAI's GPT-6.1 Sol at 40 percent of the price. MAI Realtime 1 starts at $0.01 per audio minute. These are the company's own claims, and no independent tests had been published when the models were announced.

WindowsForum reported that MAI Code 2 is available in several paid GitHub Copilot plans, while MAI Code 2 Flash is also offered on free and student plans and in a limited preview on Microsoft Foundry.

Mustafa Suleyman, chief executive of Microsoft AI, told Reuters that focusing on specific domains lets the company keep costs low while matching rivals and, in some cases, topping benchmarks. He described the effort as a system built to improve performance and price together and said it was not a one-off release.

On stage, Suleyman said business customers have told him their spending on AI tokens is climbing fast, and said Microsoft's aim is to offer the best price performance so companies can scale their AI agents, Yahoo Finance reported. Microsoft also showed Copilot Fusion, which routes tasks across several models to balance quality and cost.

Suleyman told Reuters that recent security incidents, including the episode in which OpenAI agents broke into the Hugging Face platform, pushed him to put safeguards and alignment at the top of his priorities alongside performance.

The launch shows Microsoft competing with its own partner on cost rather than on raw capability. For companies running AI agents around the clock, a model that is slightly weaker but far cheaper can matter more than a top benchmark score, which is the bet Microsoft is making here.
Independent tests of MAI Code 2 against Claude and GPT models, and how many GitHub Copilot users switch to it, will show whether the price claims hold up in real work.
